title: Global Research Trends in Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Research: A Bibliometric Analysis
content: Background/Objectives: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of acute respiratory infections and has long posed challenges to vaccine development because of historical safety concerns and the complexity of protective immunity. Recent advances in structural biology, maternal immunization, vaccines for older adults, and monoclonal antibodies have reshaped this field. This study aimed to analyze global research trends in RSV vaccine research using a bibliometric approach. Methods: A bibliometric study was conducted using records retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on April 1, 2026. Original articles and reviews published between 1968 and 2026 were selected through a title-based search strategy related to RSV and vaccination. Bibliometric indicators, citation patterns, collaboration networks, source distribution, and thematic structures were analyzed using Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny in R. Results: The final sample included 1,455 documents from 394 sources, with an annual growth rate of 8.7%. Scientific production increased markedly after 2010, with stronger acceleration after 2020. The United States led global output, followed by China, the United Kingdom, Canada, and the Netherlands. Vaccine was the most productive and locally influential source. Citation analysis identified the formalin-inactivated RSV vaccine studies from 1969 and the prefusion F protein study from 2013 as major intellectual milestones. Keyword analysis showed a shift from disease burden, epidemiology, and pathogenesis toward immunization, immunogenicity, maternal vaccination, older adults, and monoclonal antibodies. Conclusions: RSV vaccine research has evolved from a historically safety-constrained field to a mature translational area focused on prevention, implementation, real-world effectiveness, and equitable access.
